texts.orig: A first observation is that the usefulness and naturalness of the behaviors triggered by the robot hinges critically on the accuracy of the inferences about attention: When the model incorrectly concludes that the participants attention is not on the robot (false-negative errors), the coordinative triggers unnecessary pauses, interjections and phrase repeats that can be disruptive and unnatu ral. The attention inference challenge includes the need to recognize both the participants visual focus of attention (which in itself is a difficult task in the wild) and cognitive attention as on task. Cognitive attention does not overlap with visual attention all the time. For example, at times participants would shift their visual attention away from the robot as leaned in and cocked their ear to listen closely. Problems in inferring attention are compounded by lower-level vision and tracking problems. pol icy being they rent existing models for language generation; gesgagement.  Beyond the   number in phrase, the current policy does not leverage information about the contents of phrases that are about to be generated. This sometimes leads to unnatural sequences, such as Excuse me! By the way; is how to automatically   coordinate  the robot's physical pointing gestures when repeating phrases or when phrases are interrupted. With respect to turn taking, problems detected in early experimentation led to an adjustment of the coordinative policy that we described earlier: the system does not move from a wait to a verbal action ifit detects that the user is likely speaking: Beyond this simple rule, we believe that the floor dynamics in the turn-taking model need to take into account the system's discontinuous production; e.g. take into account the fact that the pauses injected within ut terances might be perceived by the participants as floor releases. Further tuning of the timings of the pauses, contingent on the dialog state and expectations about when the attention might return; as well as a tighter integration with the engagement model might be required. For instance, we ob served cases where the robot's decision to pause to wait for a participant's attention to return from the direction that the robot was pointing (before continuing to the next phrase) was interpreted as the end of the utterance and the participant walked away before session completion.
